title: Containerd process loads one CPU core up to 100% while idle
body: Recently I have twice seen containerd load one CPU core up to 100% like a busy loop, including while no containers or Docker images were present. It can begin hours after containerd boots, and I notice it from the fan noise and temperature increase. Attaching gdb and then exiting makes the load calm down. The system is Arch Linux x86_64 with kernel 6.14.5-arch1-1 and containerd v2.0.5. I captured a service log with a Go stack dump, a gdb backtrace of all threads, and the corresponding goroutine stack; thread 8 was the thread consuming the CPU. Containerd should not consume an entire CPU core for a long time while idle.

symptoms_visible: Containerd sometimes consumes 100% of one CPU core for a long time even though I have no containers or Docker images.
The episode can begin hours after containerd boots, and attaching gdb makes the CPU load drop immediately.
N0.label: N0 intermittent containerd CPU spin reported

symptoms_visible: Attaching gdb or strace makes the current CPU spike stop immediately, but containerd later starts spinning again.
N1_x.label: N1_x transient debugger workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: The CPU spike stops as soon as I connect to containerd's debug socket to capture a profile.
The episodes often start while another unrelated process is using substantial CPU, such as a compilation or a browser page running heavy JavaScript.
N1.label: N1 pprof capture perturbs the episode

symptoms_visible: Repeated containerd episodes still peg one core, but profiling or tracing the process immediately changes the behavior.
I later found dockerd spinning in the same way with no containers running.
N2.label: N2 syscall pattern and cross-process reproduction collected

symptoms_visible: On affected Linux 6.14.4 through 6.14.6 systems, unrelated processes including containerd, dockerd, rclone, gopls and lxd have been seen consuming an entire core in a similar way.
N3.label: N3 Linux kernel regression correlation established

symptoms_visible: After updating to kernel 6.14.9, I did not see containerd peg a CPU core again during three days of observation; another affected system remained stable during heavy containerd and rclone use.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved after fixed kernel update

question_patterns: Can you enable containerd's debug socket and capture a CPU profile with ctr pprof while the spike is occurring?
Please set the debug address to /run/containerd/debug.sock and run ctr --address=/run/containerd/debug.sock pprof profile when containerd starts consuming a core.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I caught it spinning and ran `ctr --address=/run/containerd/debug.sock pprof profile > profile.log`. I attached the profile, but containerd calmed down immediately when I ran the command.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profile captured the full spike without changing it and showed nearly all CPU time inside a containerd plugin function.
I captured the same profile to a different filename, and connecting to the debug socket still made the spike stop.

edges.comment: Real thread c1-c8: the reporter needed exact Go pprof instructions. Connecting through the debug socket itself stopped the active spin, so the raw profile did not reliably sample the hot state.

solution.intent: Treat attaching gdb or strace as the resolution because it immediately makes the current CPU spike stop.
solution.concrete_example: When containerd pegs a core, attach and detach gdb or strace to make it calm down.

edges.comment: The reporter repeatedly observed that attaching a debugger, tracer or pprof client stopped only the current episode. Later episodes recurred, so this perturbation is not a durable fix.

question_patterns: Since the debugger workaround is temporary, can you capture a pprof CPU profile through containerd's debug socket during the next occurrence?
Please collect `ctr pprof profile` output the next time the CPU spike returns.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It happened again, so I ran `ctr --address=/run/containerd/debug.sock pprof profile > profile.log`. The CPU load dropped as soon as the command connected.

edges.comment: Recovery from the transient-workaround branch. The recurrence establishes that debugger attachment did not resolve the underlying issue.

question_patterns: Can you collect additional profiles from later occurrences to see whether the same hot stack appears?
Please provide another pprof capture if the issue reproduces.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I captured profile2.log, profile3.log and profile4.log from later occurrences. Each time, connecting to collect the profile changed the behavior, so I could not keep the busy loop active while profiling.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: All repeated profiles consistently show containerd application code consuming the CPU, and profiling no longer stops the spike.

question_patterns: Can you trace the hot thread during another occurrence and paste the syscalls it is making?
What does strace show immediately before the CPU spike stops?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The trace includes `epoll_pwait(..., [], 128, 0, NULL, 0) = 0`, futex wake and wait calls, eventfd writes, and in a later run `nanosleep({tv_sec=0, tv_nsec=3000}, NULL) = 0`. Attaching strace again made the process calm down.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The hot thread is continuously reading and transforming container metadata files, with no epoll or futex calls.
The same zero-timeout epoll and futex sequence appears, but the nanosleep duration is slightly different.

edges.comment: Real thread c9-c17: repeated pprof captures remained inconclusive because observation stopped the spin. The reporter later supplied raw syscall lines and independently observed the same symptom in dockerd, whose gdb stack was in EpollWait.

question_patterns: Has the same one-core spin appeared in any process other than containerd?
Are other users seeing a similar symptom in unrelated applications?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I saw dockerd spin with the same symptoms and no containers running. Across our affected systems, similar episodes also appeared in rclone, gopls and lxd, and one report involved a non-Go process.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No other process is affected, and every occurrence is isolated to the same containerd plugin operation.

question_patterns: What kernel versions are the other affected systems running?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The affected Arch systems are on 6.14.4, 6.14.5 or 6.14.6.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same behavior is equally reproducible on kernels from several older release series, with no concentration in Linux 6.14.
The reports cover 6.14.4 through 6.14.7 rather than ending at 6.14.6.

question_patterns: Did the problem occur before the recent kernel upgrades?
Which earlier 6.14 kernel versions were working before this began?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I only started noticing it recently. Another affected system's package log shows upgrades from 6.14.1 to 6.14.3, then to 6.14.4 and 6.14.6; it had been fine on either 6.14.1 or 6.14.3.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It was already happening regularly on 6.14.1 and continued unchanged through every later update.

question_patterns: Do the syscall pattern and affected kernel range correspond to a recent upstream kernel change?
Can you check recent Linux changes related to epoll or eventpoll?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I found this upstream Linux commit that looks relevant: `7631dca012593c95d36199082546a24a0058fc50`.

question_patterns: Was that upstream kernel change corrected by a later commit?
Is there an upstream fix for the suspected eventpoll regression?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The correcting commit appears to be `d9ec73301099ec5975505e1c3effbe768bab9490`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I could not find any later kernel commit correcting the suspected change.

edges.comment: Real thread c15-c20: reports from multiple affected users are folded into one simulated user side. The raw evidence spans unrelated processes and Linux 6.14.4-6.14.6, directing diagnosis away from containerd application code.

solution.intent: Update from the affected Linux 6.14 kernel to a kernel containing upstream fix d9ec733, such as Arch Linux 6.14.9, then monitor under normal and heavy workloads before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Install kernel 6.14.9-arch1-1 or another kernel containing `d9ec73301099ec5975505e1c3effbe768bab9490`, reboot into it, and watch containerd and other affected processes for several days under representative load.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw epoll/futex traces, the affected kernel range, cross-process observations and upstream commit links. Concluding that the 2025 incident is the Linux eventpoll regression fixed by d9ec733—and that containerd is only one affected epoll user—is the engineering inference grounded in that evidence.

edges.comment: Resolution per c21-c23: the reporter installed 6.14.9-arch1-1 and saw no recurrence for three days; another affected user reported stable heavy containerd and rclone use on 6.14.9-zen1-1. The later Raspberry Pi report on kernel 6.18 presents materially different profiling evidence and is not evidence that the resolved 2025 kernel regression persisted.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the resolved 2025 root cause as a Linux kernel eventpoll/epoll regression affecting 6.14-era kernels, fixed by upstream commit d9ec73301099ec5975505e1c3effbe768bab9490, rather than a containerd application busy loop.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: zero-timeout epoll/futex syscall activity, observation perturbing the spin, similar behavior across unrelated processes, and concentration on Linux 6.14.4 through 6.14.6.
Must recommend updating to a kernel release containing the eventpoll fix, rather than requiring a containerd code or configuration change.
Must not present attaching gdb, strace or pprof as a durable fix; those actions only stopped the current episode and the symptom later recurred.
Must ask the user to monitor and verify behavior on the updated kernel before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Linux user and developer comfortable with systemd units, gdb, strace, kernel configuration, syscall traces and installing alternate kernels, but unfamiliar with Go's pprof workflow and needing exact commands.
persona_hint.communication_style: Methodical and evidence-driven; supplies raw traces and repeated captures, clearly notes observer effects, questions premature conclusions, and follows up after several days of verification.
